title: Who Is Liking Your Divoom Art?
h1: Who is liking your Divoom art?
lede: About half of the likes on new artworks in the Divoom app come from 2,000 accounts that are not people. This page shows how servoom found them, what they do, and why we are certain.
verdict_1: The Divoom gallery has a block of exactly {{n_accounts}} accounts that were created together, filled with copied artworks, and switched on to like everything a little. They gave {{pct_block_new}}% of all likes on new uploads in the week we watched, and about two thirds of the likes on the whole catalog today.
verdict_2: They are not people. Each of the five sections below would be enough on its own to show that. Who runs them is a separate question; the evidence points to Divoom's own servers, and we explain why at the end.
tile_accounts_s: every even-numbered id from {{id_lo}} to {{id_hi}}; the odd ids in between were never given to anyone
tile_arts_s: every one a copy of an artwork a real user uploaded in 2017 or 2018
tile_likes_s: 5 to 9 October 2026, measured on the public like lists of {{n_watched}} fresh artworks
tile_robot: comments the server marks as robot comments
tile_robot_s: out of {{n_comments_read}} comments read; every one came from a block account
how_1: Divoom is a company that sells small pixel displays. Its app has a gallery where owners post pixel art and like and comment on each other's work. Every account has a number, its user id, and every artwork has a number too. Those numbers are given out in order, so they work like a timestamp: a higher number means a newer account or upload.
how_2: servoom is an independent, volunteer project that reads the gallery's public data and publishes statistics about it. Everything on this page comes from information the app shows to any logged-in user. No private data was accessed.
ex_label: What a block account looks like
ex_1: A Divoom user asked servoom about an account called Drew that had liked their work. Drew is user {{drew_id}}. The profile looks ordinary at first: a toast avatar, level 1, 514 points, 350 likes received, 20 followers, 15 pixel artworks. Then the details stop making sense.
ex_li1: Drew follows nobody and has never commented on anything, but hands out about 500 likes every few days to hundreds of different artists.
ex_li2: All 15 of Drew's artworks are dated 2018, although the account's id number places its creation in November 2020.
ex_li3: Eleven of them are byte-for-byte identical to artworks other users uploaded in 2018, with the same title and the same upload time to the second. The other four are the same kind of copy; their originals have since been deleted.
ex_li4: Drew's user id is an even number between {{id_lo}} and {{id_hi}}. So are the ids of 1,999 other accounts that look exactly like this.
ex_caption: Three of Drew's artworks (left) next to the originals (right), with the original artist's name and the shared upload time.
e1_h2: They were made in one batch
e1_1: Divoom gives each new account the next free id number. Odd numbers go to people who sign up through the international app, even numbers to the Chinese app. Around late 2020, about 87 of every 100 odd numbers belong to a real account and about 30 of every 100 even numbers do, because sign-ups are never perfectly dense.
e1_2: Inside the range {{id_lo}} to {{id_hi}} that pattern vanishes. All 2,000 even numbers exist and none of the 2,000 odd numbers do. A run of 4,000 ids was set aside and filled in one pass. No amount of people signing up one at a time could produce this.
e1_fig: Share of account ids that are in use, in slices of 400 ids
e1_cap: Every id from 400,961,852 to 400,985,851 was looked up on 4 October 2026. The flat section in the middle is the block.
e2_h2: Every artwork they own is a copy
e2_1: On {{crawl_date}} the block's {{n_with_arts}} accounts that show any artwork held {{n_arts}} public artworks between them. Those artworks point to only {{n_files}} distinct files. Each file appears in about {{copies_mean}} accounts.
e2_2: Every copy keeps the upload time of the original, down to the second, between December 2017 and September 2018. We found the originals for many of them: early uploads by real users, posted years before the block existed. A sample is shown below, with the original artist's name.
e2_3: The copies also carry even-numbered artwork ids from {{gid_lo}} to {{gid_hi}}, and those ids run in step with the account ids: the first account holds the first few, the next account the next few. Real uploads with ids in that range date from November and December 2020. So the copies were inserted then, account by account, and labelled 2018. Divoom's upload function does not let a user choose an upload date.
e2_fig: Copies in block accounts (left) and the originals they were copied from (right)
e2_cap: Each pair is the same file: identical size and identical checksum. Originals belong to their artists and are shown only for comparison.
e3_h2: The profiles were filled in, not lived in
e3_1: A real gallery account is built up by using it. These were set up to look used. Every one of the 2,000 has a custom pixel avatar and a Western-style nickname, a level between 0 and 14, a score between 10 and 1,079 spread out evenly as if drawn at random, and between 17 and 107 followers. Nobody has zero followers. Nobody has a bio. Not one of them follows anyone.
e3_2: Their declared countries are spread evenly over {{n_countries}} countries and territories, about ten accounts each, including places like Christmas Island and Gibraltar. Real Divoom users are concentrated in China, the United States, Russia, Germany and Japan.
e3_table: The block compared with 12,404 randomly chosen real accounts
e3_mosaic: All {{n_avatars}} avatars of the block, first frame of each
e3_mosaic_cap: Every account got its own animated pixel avatar. Hover or tap one to see the account's name and id. {{n_missing_av}} avatars could not be loaded.
e4_h2: They like the way a machine likes
e4_1: From 5 to 9 October 2026 servoom read the like lists of every new upload several times a day. In those five days {{n_block_active}} of the 2,000 accounts liked something. Together they gave {{n_block_likes}} of the {{n_new_likes}} new likes we saw ({{pct_block_new}}%). All the other likes came from {{n_other_likers}} different accounts.
e4_2: In the like lists servoom read in early October, every block account appears between {{bf_min}} and {{bf_max}} times, average {{bf_mean}}. Real users are nothing like this: half of the people who like something in a month like exactly one artwork, and the most active real user in the month gave about 1,300 likes. The block has no fans and no favourites. It is one program spreading its likes evenly over 2,000 names.
e4_li1: Everything, a little. 99% of artworks uploaded in a month get at least one block like, usually one to three per visit, and the likes keep coming for weeks after real users have moved on.
e4_li2: Random name each time. Consecutive block likes on an artwork come from unrelated ids. There are no personas with tastes.
e4_li3: No views attached. A third of the artworks that receive a block like get no new view at all at the same time. The like counter moves, the view counter does not.
e4_li4: Often alone. On artworks more than a year old, about seven in ten of the latest likes are from the block, and the block likes its own copies too: two thirds of the likes on block-owned artworks come from other block accounts.
e4_li5: Quiet for years, then switched on. The accounts existed from late 2020, but more than nine in ten of their likes that we could date happened after June 2025. Today they give around 10,000 likes a day, roughly five per account.
e4_fig: Where one week's likes on fresh uploads came from
e4_cap: {{n_new_likes}} likes on uploads from the first days of October 2026, read from the public like lists. The block is 2,000 accounts; "everyone else" is {{n_other_likers}} accounts.
e5_h2: Divoom's own server calls them robots
e5_1: Every comment in the gallery carries a hidden field named RobertFlag, a misspelling of "robot flag". The app never shows it, but the server sends it. In {{n_comments_read}} recent comments servoom read, {{n_robot}} had the flag set to 1. All {{n_robot}} were written by block accounts, in August and September 2021, by accounts with consecutive ids, one every one to three hours, under the same artworks.
e5_2: The texts are stock praise, some of it lifted from somewhere else and pasted where it makes no sense. In March and April 2026 the block ran a second campaign of about 380 comments, this time without the flag. It has not commented since.
e5_fig: A 2021 comment campaign on one artwork, as the server returns it today
e5_cap: Artwork {{robot_gid}}, a popular 2021 character piece. The accounts are the block's ids 400,975,312 to 400,975,320 and 400,973,446 to 400,973,464, two apart, posting in order.
e5_fig2: The 2026 campaign: comments from block accounts on one artwork, not flagged
tl_1: Real early users upload the {{n_files}} artworks that will later be copied.
tl_2: The block is created: 2,000 accounts on a reserved id range, with copied artworks labelled 2018, avatars, names, scores and followers.
tl_3: First comment campaign. The server stores these comments with its robot flag set.
tl_4: Almost no activity. Only a few percent of likes on artworks from these years come from the block.
tl_5: Liking ramps up to around 10,000 likes a day.
tl_6: Second comment campaign, about 380 comments, not flagged.
tl_7: The block gives {{pct_block_new}}% of likes on new uploads and most of the likes on old ones. This report.
sure_h2: Certain that they are not people
sure_1: Each line of evidence is independent of the others, and each one alone rules out 2,000 ordinary users: nobody can register on ids that were never offered, upload a file at the exact second a stranger did years earlier, or like 500 artworks every few days without ever viewing one. Together they describe one automated system wearing 2,000 names.
sure_2: What we cannot see is anyone's intent, the code that drives the accounts, or activity on Divoom's separate Chinese servers. Our counts are measurements of a sample of the gallery and carry a margin of a few percent. None of that changes the conclusion.
who_0: This part is an inference, not a measurement. We lay out the possibilities and what the evidence says about each.
who_1: Only the server gives out id numbers, and it skipped 2,000 odd ones while filling the even ones. Only the server can store an artwork under another user's file with a 2018 date. Only the server sets the robot flag on comments. Scores, medals and followers exist without any activity to earn them. Everything the block has was granted, not done.
who_2: An outsider can register accounts and press the like button, but cannot reserve an id range, copy files under old dates, or set a server flag. Paid likes also go to whoever paid; these go to everyone, a little.
who_3: The accounts are active today, their volume grew through 2025 and 2026, and their comment campaigns changed form between 2021 and 2026. Somebody is operating them.
who_4: We found no statement from Divoom about these accounts. The purpose is easy to guess: a gallery where every upload gets a few likes within days looks friendlier than one where most uploads get none. But a like that comes from a program tells an artist nothing.
you_li1: A like from any even-numbered account between {{id_lo}} and {{id_hi}} is not a person's opinion. Use the list at the end of this page to check an account that liked or followed you.
you_li2: For a new artwork, roughly half of its likes are from the block. For an artwork more than a year old, most of them are.
you_li3: Comments, and likes from accounts that also post their own work, are the honest signal. Views appear to be unaffected by the block.
you_li4: Blocking these accounts in the app only hides their likes from you. It does not change the counters anyone else sees.
ask_1: Divoom's users deserve to know whether the likes they receive are real. We ask Divoom to say who operates these 2,000 accounts and why, to label or remove their likes and comments, and to confirm that no other such accounts exist. If you agree, share this page and ask them too.

method_li1: Profiles. Every account id within 10,000 of the block and every 500th id pair across the whole id range (44,007 lookups, 4 October 2026); all 2,000 block profiles again on 9 October 2026, with their avatars and full artwork lists.
method_li2: Likes. The complete public like lists of every artwork uploaded between 5 and 9 October 2026, read several times a day; full like lists of 2,440 artworks spread across all years; the latest likes on the whole public catalog, read on 5 and 7 October 2026.
method_li3: Artworks. A crawl of every public category of the gallery (about 1.05 million artworks still public on 7 October 2026) gives the originals' upload times; matching files were downloaded and compared byte by byte.
method_li4: Comments. 13,423 comments on artworks commented on in September 2026, plus the comment lists of the campaign artworks, re-read on 9 October 2026.
method_li5: Limits. Likes carry no timestamp, so their dates are lower bounds from list order. Private and deleted uploads are not counted. The Chinese app servers were not examined. Counts from samples are good to a few percent.
method_li6: Everything was read with throwaway accounts that never liked, followed, commented or uploaded.
about_1: servoom is an independent open-source project that documents the Divoom gallery and publishes community statistics. It is not affiliated with Divoom. Source code and methods are public at servoom.pages.dev. Questions and corrections are welcome there.
